subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Apply Newton's three laws of motion
Forces as interactions between two bodies
Find the resultant force from a free-body diagram
Use normal, friction, tension, elastic, drag and buoyancy forces
Use gravitational, electric and magnetic field forces
Momentum and when it is conserved
Impulse as average resultant force times contact time
Impulse equals the change in momentum
Why F = Δp/Δt is more general than F = ma
Kinetic energy in collisions and explosions
Centripetal force is the resultant force towards the centre
A centripetal force changes direction, not speed
Link angular velocity, period and linear speed

questions.q: An ice-hockey puck is struck and then slides across horizontal ice. Friction and air resistance on the puck are negligible. What happens to the motion of the puck after it has left the stick?
options: It slows gradually as the force from the stick is used up.
It continues in a straight line at a constant speed.
It slows and stops, as moving bodies come to rest naturally.
It stops at once, since nothing now pushes it along its path.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the stick gives the puck a store of 'force' that runs out picks this. A force exists only while the stick touches the puck. Once contact ends there is no force from the stick, and with negligible friction nothing slows the puck.

Newton's first law: with no resultant force, the velocity of the puck is constant, so it moves in a straight line at constant speed. The stick exerted a force only while in contact; no force is needed to keep the puck moving.

A student who believes that rest is the natural state of every body picks this. Everyday objects stop because friction and drag act on them. Here these are negligible, so by Newton's first law the puck keeps its velocity.

A student who believes a moving body needs a force in its direction of motion picks this. Newton's first law says a force is needed to CHANGE velocity, not to maintain it. With no resultant force, the puck keeps moving.
questions.explain: Newton's first law: with no resultant force, the velocity of the puck is constant, so it moves in a straight line at constant speed. The stick exerted a force only while in contact; no force is needed to keep the puck moving.

questions.q: A book rests on a horizontal table. The weight of the book is the gravitational force exerted on it by the Earth. Which force forms a Newton's third law pair with this weight?
options: The normal force exerted on the book by the table
The contact force exerted on the table by the book
The gravitational force exerted on the Earth by the book
No force, because the book is too small to pull the Earth
optionWhy: A student who pairs any two equal and opposite forces picks this. The normal force and the weight both act on the book and come from different interactions (contact and gravitational). They balance because the book is in equilibrium, which is Newton's first law, not the third.

A student who thinks the book's push on the table is its weight picks this. That push is a contact force: it forms a third-law pair with the table's normal force on the book. The weight is gravitational, so its partner is gravitational too: the book's pull on the Earth.

A third-law pair is the two forces of ONE interaction, here the gravitational interaction between the book and the Earth. The Earth pulls the book down; the book pulls the Earth up with a force of equal magnitude. The two forces are of the same type and act on different bodies.

A student who thinks a small body cannot exert a force on a massive one picks this. The book pulls the Earth with a force equal in magnitude to its weight. The Earth's resulting acceleration is negligible because its mass is enormous, not because the force is absent.
questions.explain: A third-law pair is the two forces of ONE interaction, here the gravitational interaction between the book and the Earth. The Earth pulls the book down; the book pulls the Earth up with a force of equal magnitude. The two forces are of the same type and act on different bodies.

questions.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. Air resistance is negligible. Which force or forces act on the ball while it is still rising, after it has left the hand?
options: Its weight and a decreasing upward force from the throw
Its weight and an upward force larger than its weight
No force until it stops at the top and then starts to fall
Only its weight, the downward pull of the Earth
optionWhy: A student who thinks the ball carries the 'force of the throw' with it picks this. The hand's force acts only during contact. After release the ball carries momentum, not force, and that upward momentum decreases because the weight acts downwards.

A student who believes a body moving upwards must have an upward resultant force picks this. The ball is slowing down, so the resultant force is downwards. Its upward motion is due to its velocity, which needs no force to continue.

A student who thinks gravity acts only on falling objects picks this. The Earth pulls on the ball throughout the flight; that is why the ball's upward velocity decreases steadily and reaches zero at the top.

Once the ball leaves the hand, the only body still interacting with it is the Earth (air resistance is negligible). Its weight acts downwards throughout the flight, which is why the ball slows as it rises.
questions.explain: Once the ball leaves the hand, the only body still interacting with it is the Earth (air resistance is negligible). Its weight acts downwards throughout the flight, which is why the ball slows as it rises.

questions.q: A box is pulled at constant velocity across a rough horizontal floor by a rope that makes an angle of 30° above the horizontal. Which list gives all the forces that should appear on a free-body diagram of the box, and no others?
options: Weight, normal force, tension, friction, push of box on floor
Weight, normal force, tension, friction, forward force of motion
Weight, normal force, rope tension and friction from the floor
Weight, tension and friction; the rigid floor exerts no push up
optionWhy: A student who draws both forces of a third-law pair on one diagram picks this. The push of the box on the floor acts ON THE FLOOR, so it belongs on the floor's free-body diagram, not the box's.

A student who thinks a moving body needs a force of its own in its direction of motion picks this. There is no 'force of motion': the box moves at constant velocity because the forward component of the tension balances friction.

A free-body diagram shows every force that other bodies exert ON the box: the Earth (weight F_g), the floor (normal force F_N and friction F_f) and the rope (tension T). Nothing else touches the box or exerts a field force on it.

A student who thinks a rigid floor is just an obstacle picks this. The floor is compressed slightly and pushes up on the box with the normal force F_N. The box presses on the floor (that is why friction acts), so F_N must appear on its free-body diagram.
questions.explain: A free-body diagram shows every force that other bodies exert ON the box: the Earth (weight F_g), the floor (normal force F_N and friction F_f) and the rope (tension T). Nothing else touches the box or exerts a field force on it.

questions.q: The diagram shows a free-body diagram drawn by a student for a block at rest on a rough slope. Which statement about the diagram is correct?
options: The diagram is correct as drawn: F_N acts vertically so that it balances W.
F_f should be removed from the diagram, because the block is not sliding.
An arrow for the push of the block on the slope is missing from the diagram.
F_N is wrongly drawn: it should be perpendicular to the surface of the slope.
optionWhy: 'Normal' means perpendicular to the surface, not vertical. On a slope F_N is tilted by 30° from the vertical and has magnitude mg cos 30°; it is F_N and F_f together, not F_N alone, that balance the weight.

Static friction acts on a stationary body whenever something tends to make it slide. Without friction the block would accelerate down the slope, so F_f (up the slope) is a real force on it and belongs on the diagram.
The push of the block on the slope acts on the slope, not on the block. A free-body diagram shows only the forces acting on the chosen body, so that force must not appear.

The normal force is the component of the contact force perpendicular to the surface, so on a slope it is tilted from the vertical by the angle of the slope. W and F_f are correctly drawn; only the direction of F_N needs changing.
questions.explain: The normal force is the component of the contact force perpendicular to the surface, so on a slope it is tilted from the vertical by the angle of the slope. W and F_f are correctly drawn; only the direction of F_N needs changing.

Three arrows start at the centre of the block: W pointing vertically downwards; F_f pointing up the slope, parallel to its surface; and F_N pointing vertically upwards, directly opposite to W.

questions.q: A free-body diagram for a puck on a frictionless horizontal air table shows three horizontal forces: 30 N towards the east, 10 N towards the west and 15 N towards the north. The vertical forces on the puck balance. What is the magnitude of the resultant force on the puck?
optionWhy: East–west: 30 N − 10 N = 20 N east. North: 15 N. These are perpendicular, so the resultant is √(20² + 15²) N = 25 N.
A student who adds the magnitudes of all the forces gets 30 + 10 + 15 = 55 N. Forces are vectors: the west force opposes the east force, and the north force is perpendicular to both.
A student who correctly finds 20 N east but then adds the perpendicular 15 N arithmetically gets 35 N. Perpendicular components combine by Pythagoras: √(20² + 15²) = 25 N.
A student who adds the east and west forces as though they pointed the same way gets 40 N, and then √(40² + 15²) = 43 N. The 10 N force acts westwards, so it subtracts from the 30 N force.
questions.explain: East–west: 30 N − 10 N = 20 N east. North: 15 N. These are perpendicular, so the resultant is √(20² + 15²) N = 25 N.
questions.working: Take east and north as positive. F_x = 30 N − 10 N = 20 N; F_y = 15 N. |F| = √(20² + 15²) N = √625 N = 25 N.

questions.q: A block of mass 4.0 kg slides down a rough plane inclined at 25° to the horizontal. The coefficient of dynamic friction between the block and the plane is 0.20. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the magnitude of the frictional force on the block?
optionWhy: A student who takes the normal force to equal the weight uses F_N = 39.2 N and gets 7.8 N. On an incline only the component of the weight perpendicular to the plane, mg cos 25°, is balanced by F_N.
Perpendicular to the plane there is no acceleration, so F_N = mg cos 25° = 4.0 × 9.8 × 0.906 = 35.5 N. The block slides, so F_f = μ_d F_N = 0.20 × 35.5 N = 7.1 N.
A student who uses mg sin 25° for the normal force gets 3.3 N. The angle between the weight and the normal to the plane is 25°, so the perpendicular component is mg cos 25°.

A student who resolves the normal force instead of the weight writes F_N cos 25° = mg, so F_N = 43.3 N and F_f = 8.7 N. Perpendicular to the plane, F_N balances the component mg cos 25°, so F_N is smaller than mg.
questions.explain: Perpendicular to the plane there is no acceleration, so F_N = mg cos 25° = 4.0 × 9.8 × 0.906 = 35.5 N. The block slides, so F_f = μ_d F_N = 0.20 × 35.5 N = 7.1 N.

questions.q: Which statement about field forces is correct?
options: A magnetic field exerts a force on a charged particle even when it is at rest.
An electric field exerts a force on a charged particle even when it is at rest.
A gravitational force acts on a body only where there is air around it.
An astronaut in orbit has no weight, as gravity does not act there.
optionWhy: A student who treats magnetic forces on charges like electric forces picks this. A magnetic field exerts a force only on a MOVING charge; a stationary charge in a magnetic field experiences no magnetic force.
An electric field exerts a force F_e on any charge in it, whether the charge is moving or stationary. This is one of the differences between the electric and the magnetic force.
A student who links gravity to the atmosphere picks this. Gravity is a field force that acts through empty space: the Sun's gravity holds the Earth in orbit across the vacuum between them.
A student who takes 'weightlessness' literally picks this. Gravity acts strongly in orbit; it provides the centripetal force that keeps the astronaut and spacecraft falling around the Earth together.
questions.explain: An electric field exerts a force F_e on any charge in it, whether the charge is moving or stationary. This is one of the differences between the electric and the magnetic force.

questions.q: Under which condition does the total momentum of a system of interacting bodies remain constant?
options: When every collision between the bodies is elastic
When the bodies exert no forces at all on one another
When no resultant external force acts on the system
When every body in the system moves at a constant speed
optionWhy: A student who links momentum conservation to kinetic-energy conservation picks this. Momentum is conserved in inelastic collisions and explosions too; elastic collisions are special only because total kinetic energy is also conserved.

A student who does not distinguish internal from external forces picks this. The bodies in a collision exert large forces on each other, but these are equal and opposite, so they cancel in the total momentum.

Forces between the bodies are internal and cancel in third-law pairs, so only an external resultant force can change the total momentum. With no resultant external force, the total momentum is constant, whatever happens inside the system.

A student who equates constant speed with constant momentum picks this. Momentum is a vector: a body moving at constant speed along a curve has changing momentum. What matters is the resultant external force on the system.
questions.explain: Forces between the bodies are internal and cancel in third-law pairs, so only an external resultant force can change the total momentum. With no resultant external force, the total momentum is constant, whatever happens inside the system.

questions.q: A cricket ball is struck by a bat. During the short time of contact the force between the bat and the ball rises from zero to a maximum and then falls back to zero. Which statement about the impulse delivered to the ball is correct?
options: It is the product of the maximum force exerted on the ball and the total time of contact.
It is the product of the average resultant force on the ball and the time of contact.
It is the largest value reached by the resultant force on the ball during the contact.
It is the average resultant force on the ball divided by the total time of contact.
optionWhy: Using the peak force as if it acted throughout overestimates the impulse. The force rises and falls, so the impulse is the average force multiplied by the time, which is the area under the force–time graph.

J = FΔt, where F is the AVERAGE resultant force over the contact time Δt. Because the force varies, its average over the contact must be used; the impulse then equals the change in momentum of the ball.
Impulse is not a force. It is force multiplied by time (unit N s), and it equals the change in momentum of the ball. The large brief force produces the impulse; it is not the impulse itself.
Dividing force by time gives a quantity with unit N s⁻¹, which is not impulse. Impulse is force MULTIPLIED by time, unit N s, and a longer contact at the same average force delivers a larger impulse.
questions.explain: J = FΔt, where F is the AVERAGE resultant force over the contact time Δt. Because the force varies, its average over the contact must be used; the impulse then equals the change in momentum of the ball.

questions.q: A ball of mass 0.060 kg moving at 30 m s⁻¹ strikes a wall at right angles and rebounds along the same line at 20 m s⁻¹. Taking the direction towards the wall as positive, what impulse does the wall exert on the ball?
optionWhy: A student who assumes the change in momentum is in the ball's original direction of motion gets the magnitude right but the sign wrong. The wall pushes the ball away from itself, so the impulse is negative.
A student who uses speeds without signs calculates 0.060 × (20 − 30) = −0.6 N s. The final velocity is −20 m s⁻¹, because the ball moves away from the wall; momentum is a vector.
A student who counts only the stopping of the ball calculates 0.060 × (0 − 30) = −1.8 N s. The wall must also push the ball back out at 20 m s⁻¹, which adds a further −1.2 N s.
Impulse = change in momentum = m(v − u) = 0.060 kg × (−20 − 30) m s⁻¹ = −3.0 N s: 3.0 N s directed away from the wall.
questions.explain: Impulse = change in momentum = m(v − u) = 0.060 kg × (−20 − 30) m s⁻¹ = −3.0 N s: 3.0 N s directed away from the wall.
questions.working: J = Δp = m(v − u) with u = +30 m s⁻¹ and v = −20 m s⁻¹: J = 0.060 kg × (−20 − 30) m s⁻¹ = 0.060 × (−50) = −3.0 N s (3.0 N s away from the wall).

questions.q: Sand falls vertically onto a horizontal conveyor belt at a steady rate of 0.80 kg s⁻¹. The belt moves at a constant 2.5 m s⁻¹, and the sand quickly reaches the speed of the belt. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the horizontal force that the belt exerts on the sand?
optionWhy: A student who applies F = ma to the belt's constant velocity gets zero. F = ma assumes constant mass. Here new sand arrives all the time and must be accelerated from rest to 2.5 m s⁻¹, so the sand's horizontal momentum increases at 2.0 kg m s⁻², which requires a horizontal force of 2.0 N.

A student who assumes all the belt's work becomes kinetic energy of the sand writes Fv = ½(Δm/Δt)v² and gets 1.0 N. While the sand slips before matching the belt's speed, friction dissipates as much energy as the sand gains, so the momentum method must be used.
The mass on the belt is changing, so F = Δp/Δt must be used. Each second, 0.80 kg of sand gains a horizontal velocity of 2.5 m s⁻¹: F = v(Δm/Δt) = 2.5 × 0.80 = 2.0 N.

A student who thinks the force needed to move sand is its weight, and treats the 0.80 kg arriving each second as the load, gets 0.80 × 9.8 = 7.8 N. The weight is vertical and is supported by the belt's normal force; the horizontal force depends only on the horizontal momentum given to the sand.
questions.explain: The mass on the belt is changing, so F = Δp/Δt must be used. Each second, 0.80 kg of sand gains a horizontal velocity of 2.5 m s⁻¹: F = v(Δm/Δt) = 2.5 × 0.80 = 2.0 N.
questions.working: F = Δp/Δt. Horizontal momentum gained per second = (Δm/Δt) × v = 0.80 kg s⁻¹ × 2.5 m s⁻¹ = 2.0 kg m s⁻² = 2.0 N. (F = ma would give zero because the belt's velocity is constant, but the mass being moved is not constant.)

questions.q: Which statement describes an elastic collision between two bodies?
options: The bodies bounce apart after colliding, instead of sticking together.
The total kinetic energy of the two bodies is the same before and after.
At least one of the bodies is made of a stretchy material such as rubber.
Momentum is conserved, which is not the case in an inelastic collision.
optionWhy: A student who equates 'elastic' with 'bouncing' picks this. Bodies can bounce apart and still lose kinetic energy; such a collision is inelastic. Only sticking together is ruled out for an elastic collision.
An elastic collision is defined by the conservation of total kinetic energy. Total momentum is conserved too, as it is in every collision of an isolated system.
A student using the everyday meaning of 'elastic' picks this. In physics the word refers to kinetic energy being conserved, whatever the materials; hard steel balls can collide almost elastically.

A student who links momentum conservation to kinetic-energy conservation picks this. Momentum is conserved in inelastic collisions as well. What distinguishes an elastic collision is the kinetic energy.
questions.explain: An elastic collision is defined by the conservation of total kinetic energy. Total momentum is conserved too, as it is in every collision of an isolated system.

questions.q: A trolley of mass 1.2 kg moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ along a straight horizontal track collides with a stationary trolley of mass 0.80 kg. The trolleys stick together. Friction is negligible. What is their speed immediately after the collision?
options: 1.5 m s⁻¹
4.5 m s⁻¹
2.3 m s⁻¹
1.8 m s⁻¹
optionWhy: A student who averages the two initial velocities, (3.0 + 0) ÷ 2, gets 1.5 m s⁻¹. That works only for equal masses; momentum conservation weights each velocity by its mass.

A student who divides the momentum by the mass of the stationary trolley alone, 3.6 ÷ 0.80, gets 4.5 m s⁻¹, faster than the trolley that hit it. The trolleys move together, so the momentum is shared by the total mass, 2.0 kg.

A student who assumes kinetic energy is conserved writes ½ × 1.2 × 3.0² = ½ × 2.0 × v² and gets 2.3 m s⁻¹. Trolleys that stick together collide inelastically; momentum, not kinetic energy, gives the final velocity.
Momentum is conserved: 1.2 × 3.0 = (1.2 + 0.80)v, so v = 3.6 ÷ 2.0 = 1.8 m s⁻¹.
questions.explain: Momentum is conserved: 1.2 × 3.0 = (1.2 + 0.80)v, so v = 3.6 ÷ 2.0 = 1.8 m s⁻¹.
questions.working: p before = 1.2 kg × 3.0 m s⁻¹ + 0 = 3.6 kg m s⁻¹. p after = (1.2 + 0.80) kg × v. v = 3.6/2.0 = 1.8 m s⁻¹, in the original direction.

questions.q: Two ice skaters stand at rest facing each other on smooth ice. Skater A, of mass 60 kg, pushes skater B, of mass 45 kg, and they move apart in opposite directions along a straight line. Immediately afterwards B moves at 2.0 m s⁻¹. Friction is negligible. What is the speed of A?
options: 2.0 m s⁻¹
1.5 m s⁻¹
1.7 m s⁻¹
0.0 m s⁻¹
optionWhy: A student who reasons that equal and opposite forces give equal speeds picks this. The forces and impulses are equal, so the MOMENTA are equal and opposite; the heavier skater therefore moves more slowly.
The total momentum is zero before the push, so it is zero after: 60 × v_A = 45 × 2.0, giving v_A = 1.5 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction to B.

A student who assumes the skaters receive equal kinetic energies writes ½ × 60 × v² = ½ × 45 × 2.0² and gets 1.7 m s⁻¹. Momentum, not kinetic energy, is shared equally in magnitude; the lighter skater receives more kinetic energy.
A student who thinks the skater who does the pushing receives no force picks this. B pushes back on A with an equal force (third law), so A recoils; total momentum stays zero only if A moves.
questions.explain: The total momentum is zero before the push, so it is zero after: 60 × v_A = 45 × 2.0, giving v_A = 1.5 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction to B.
questions.working: Total momentum before = 0. After: m_A v_A + m_B v_B = 0 ⇒ 60 kg × v_A = −45 kg × 2.0 m s⁻¹ ⇒ v_A = −1.5 m s⁻¹, a speed of 1.5 m s⁻¹ opposite to B.

questions.q: A firework shell is at rest when it explodes into several fragments. External forces can be ignored during the explosion. Which statement about the fragments immediately after the explosion is correct?
options: Their total momentum has increased, as has their total kinetic energy.
Their total momentum is zero, and so is their total kinetic energy.
Their total momentum is zero and their total kinetic energy has increased.
Their total momentum is zero, and the total energy of the system has risen.
optionWhy: A student who thinks motion from rest means new momentum picks this. Momentum is a vector: the fragments fly off in different directions and their momenta add to zero, the value before the explosion.
A student who treats kinetic energy as a vector picks this. Kinetic energy ½mv² is a scalar and is never negative, so the fragments' kinetic energies add; only momenta can cancel.

The explosive forces are internal, so the total momentum stays zero: the fragments' momenta cancel as vectors. Chemical energy is transferred to kinetic energy, so the total kinetic energy, zero before, has increased.
A student who thinks explosions create energy picks this. The kinetic energy comes from the chemical energy stored in the explosive; the total energy of the system is unchanged.
questions.explain: The explosive forces are internal, so the total momentum stays zero: the fragments' momenta cancel as vectors. Chemical energy is transferred to kinetic energy, so the total kinetic energy, zero before, has increased.

questions.q: The drum of a washing machine has a diameter of 0.50 m. It rotates about a horizontal axis at constant speed, with a time period of 0.050 s. What is the centripetal acceleration of a sock pressed against the inside of the drum?
optionWhy: A student who takes a to be inversely proportional to T, as v is, calculates 4π² × 0.25/0.050 = 2.0 × 10². Check the units: m ÷ s is not an acceleration; the period must be squared.
A student who substitutes the diameter, 0.50 m, as r gets twice the correct acceleration. The equation uses the radius, 0.25 m.
A student who calculates 2πr/T = 31 gives the speed of the sock, 31 m s⁻¹, not its acceleration. The acceleration is v²/r = 31.4²/0.25 = 3.9 × 10³ m s⁻².
r = 0.25 m. a = 4π²r/T² = 4π² × 0.25/(0.050)² = 3.9 × 10³ m s⁻², directed towards the axis of the drum.
questions.explain: r = 0.25 m. a = 4π²r/T² = 4π² × 0.25/(0.050)² = 3.9 × 10³ m s⁻², directed towards the axis of the drum.
questions.working: r = 0.50 m/2 = 0.25 m. a = 4π²r/T² = 4π² × 0.25 m/(0.050 s)² = 9.87 m/2.5 × 10⁻³ s² = 3.9 × 10³ m s⁻². (Equivalently v = 2πr/T = 31.4 m s⁻¹ and a = v²/r = 3.9 × 10³ m s⁻².)

questions.q: A car travels at constant speed around a bend on a flat horizontal road; its path is part of a horizontal circle. Air resistance is negligible. Which statement about the horizontal forces on the car is correct?
options: Friction from the road acts towards the centre and is the resultant force.
Friction acts towards the centre and is balanced by a centrifugal force.
Friction and a separate centripetal force both act towards the centre.
A forward driving force along the bend is the resultant force on the car.
optionWhy: On a flat road the only horizontal force towards the centre is friction between the tyres and the road. With air resistance negligible, no force is needed along the path at constant speed, so this friction is the resultant force and provides the centripetal force mv²/r.

A student who believes in a real outward force picks this. If friction were balanced, the resultant would be zero and the car would travel in a straight line. There is no outward force on the car; the resultant is inwards.

A student who treats centripetal force as an extra force picks this. 'Centripetal force' is the name for the resultant towards the centre, and here that resultant IS the friction. It is not a second force.

A student who thinks motion needs a resultant force in its direction picks this. At constant speed there is no resultant force along the path. The resultant is towards the centre, perpendicular to the velocity, and changes only the car's direction.
questions.explain: On a flat road the only horizontal force towards the centre is friction between the tyres and the road. With air resistance negligible, no force is needed along the path at constant speed, so this friction is the resultant force and provides the centripetal force mv²/r.

questions.q: A cyclist rides around a flat circular track at a constant speed of 8.0 m s⁻¹. Which statement about her motion is correct?
options: Her velocity is constant, so the resultant force acting on her is zero.
Her velocity changes, so a resultant force acts towards the centre.
A resultant force acts on her outwards, away from the centre of the track.
A resultant force acts on her forwards, along her direction of motion.
optionWhy: A student who treats constant speed as constant velocity picks this. The direction of her motion keeps changing, so her velocity changes and a resultant force must act.

Velocity is a vector. Her speed is constant but the direction of her velocity changes continuously, so she accelerates towards the centre and, by Newton's second law, a resultant force acts towards the centre.

A student who believes in a real centrifugal force picks this. An outward resultant force would make her curve away from the centre. The resultant force is inwards; the outward 'feeling' is her tendency to continue in a straight line.

A student who thinks motion needs a force along it picks this. A forward resultant force would increase her speed, but her speed is constant. The resultant is perpendicular to her velocity, towards the centre.

questions.q: A bicycle wheel of diameter 0.700 m rotates at a steady rate about a fixed axle, making one complete revolution every 0.250 s. What is the linear speed of a point on the rim of the wheel?
optionWhy: A student who substitutes the diameter as r gets twice the correct speed. In one revolution the rim travels a circumference, 2πr = π × diameter = 2.20 m.
A student who divides the radius by the period gets 0.350 ÷ 0.250 = 1.40 m s⁻¹. In one period the point travels round the whole circumference, 2πr, not a distance r.
A student who stops at ω = 2π/T = 25.1 has found the angular velocity, in rad s⁻¹. The linear speed is v = ωr = 25.1 × 0.350 = 8.80 m s⁻¹.
